identity.name: SBI CARDS & PAY SER LTD
identity.industry: Financial Services / Credit Cards & Consumer Payments — pure-play credit-card issuer (NBFC), SBI subsidiary

summary.oneLiner: i.e. essentially all of the profit growth came from the provisioning line

one-line thesis: A clean credit-cost-led earnings recovery: gross credit cost fell 301 bps YoY to 6.5%, GNPA −102 bps YoY to 2.04% and NNPA 0.83% ("the lowest since Q3 of FY23"), pushing PAT to INR664 crores, up 20% Y-o-Y on revenue that grew only 3% Y-o-Y — i.e. essentially all of the profit growth came from the provisioning line, not the topline. Spends hit a record INR1,18,475 crores (+27% YoY) with spend market share up to 19.5% vs 18.1% in FY26, but receivables grew just ~2% QoQ / 3% YoY to INR58,269 crores and management explicitly pushed asset growth out: "We expect asset growth to pick up from the second half of financial year 2027." The open question for FY27 is whether yield/NIM (portfolio yield 16%, NIM 10.8%, ROA 3.9%) can hold while cost of funds is guided "to trend higher in line with the market rates" and personal loans cannibalise the revolver.
financial scorecard (track qoq/yoy): > All figures as stated by management on the call. No ratio has been computed here; where a period-on-period delta is shown, management stated that delta.
> One-offs / accounting distortions — call these out explicitly:

> 1. Annual ECL model review completed in Q1 FY27 — "INR180 crores have been consumed out of INR220 crores overlay of the previous quarter." This is the single biggest distortion in the quarter: the credit-cost improvement is partly an overlay drawdown, not purely organic flow improvement. ECL rates rose QoQ for Stage 1 and Stage 3 as a result of the refresh (analyst-observed, management did not dispute).
> 2. Provision release of INR65 crores "with improved portfolio mix during the quarter."

> 3. Residual management overlay INR70 crores carried forward "keeping in view the current geopolitical uncertainties" — CRO confirmed "INR70 crores, we are just carrying it for the Stage 1. It is in Stage 1 only."
> 4. Write-back of INR35 crores on account of good asset quality for the quarter (CRO, referring to the presentation) — "asset quality or provision for Stage 2, 3 is not part of that [the INR70 cr]."

> 5. New wage code past-service cost inflated employee opex QoQ — "the employee opex increase in this quarter is on the account of the provision increase in our past services cost, the liability that has been added on account of the change in the new wage code." Not quantified on this call.
> 6. Instance-based fee income is depressed by lower late fees — "the instance-based fees is down primarily, the reason is late fees."
guidance (critical — verify next quarter: Management repeatedly and explicitly refused numeric guidance this quarter: "we are not giving any guidance in terms of the numbers" (EMI); "As of now, I'm not giving any guidance in terms of the numbers" / "I'm refraining from giving any guidance in terms of the absolute numbers or percentage terms right now" (credit cost, receivables). What was given:

Receivables / asset growth: "We expect asset growth to pick up from the second half of financial year 2027, given higher new acquisition from this quarter onwards and festive season in Q3"; restated in Q&A — "in the second half of this year, we will see growth in receivables as well." (H2 FY27 = Oct-2026 → Mar-2027.)

Credit cost: "this trend of credit cost, will see some more moderation going forward"; on a peer's 3Q normalisation comment — "Normalization can be debated. But definitely, as I mentioned, we will moderate further in terms of credit cost." Caveated: "we expect the gross credit cost to stay within the current range, subject to any adverse impact of Middle East conflict on the asset quality."
ROA: "on track to achieve our stated ROA guidance of 4% to 4.5% in medium term" (medium-term, no date).
NIM: "I would say NIM should be around this range only… we should maintain the NIM around these levels."
Portfolio yield: "as we had guided that we will continue to keep the yield in a broad range."

Cost of funds: "we don't expect much change. It should remain somewhere in the similar range. Ultimately, it will depend to a very large extent on the policy action as well in terms of the T-bill rates" — but the prepared remarks said "we expect cost of funds to trend higher in line with the market rates." These two statements sit in tension; treat the prepared-remark version as the base case and flag it next quarter.

Cost-to-income: "We'll give you a yearly number, which is an average of all the 4 quarters. So it should be… in the range of about 56% to 58%" (FY27 full-year; reaffirming last quarter's indication). Q3 will be seasonally worse — "obviously, the festive season will definitely see a higher cost to income."

Corporate spend mix: "we would like it to be around 20% of our overall spend… It will be 20% plus minus"; can go below 20% — "We can take it below 20% also. We like to keep most of our spends profitable."
Revolver: "we expect the revolver to continue to be stable where they are right now… we have witnessed a little bit of a downward bias on the revolver. But they will stay in somewhat similar range."
Instance-based fees: "Once the base effect starts to come in, in H2 onwards, you will start seeing it go up but not on account of late fee. Late fee will continue to remain at the level that it is."
Opex: "we do expect that as the festive season comes in, these expenses will be higher."

ECL model: "Normally, we will not relax the model. At most, we may do some kind of an enhancement… Whatever changes will happen during the year will happen because of the data refresh" — i.e. any FY28 ECL tailwind comes from data refresh, not model loosening.
order book & pipeline: Not an order-book business. Forward pipeline proxies disclosed on the call:

New-account run-rate: >1 million new accounts in Q1 FY27 (+17% YoY); net card additions of 4.84 lakh, "highest in the industry for the quarter" per RBI data — the acquisition cohort that management says converts to receivables growth in H2 FY27.

Addressable market (two-legged, management's own framing): (a) Banca / "family silver" — SBI has "almost 53 crores plus customers", of which "you still end up with at least 1.5 crores to 2 crores customers of the bank, which are cardable", plus corporate salary-package and home-loan bases; (b) open market — co-brands, e.g. "Flipkart itself has close to more than 500 million customers on their transacting customers."

Bureau-scoreable universe: "there are at least 350 million to 400 million customers, where the files – and where the data is available, you can credit score those customers", against "India now has 121 million credit cards in circulation" and "We have hardly 52 million to 55 million customers in the country."
Co-brand milestone: "our core brand BPCL SBI Card crossed the 5 million milestone, making it one of the largest fuel co-branded credit card partnerships in India."
segment / subsidiary detail: Retail cards — the entire profit pool. "On an overall basis, in the absolute sense, the corporate card profitability is very low. Our profits are essentially on the retail card." Retail earns both fee and interest income.

Corporate / commercial cards — interchange-only, deliberately capped. "In corporate card spends, typically — we don't give lending options there. So the customer has to pay back the full outstanding balance. So primary source of income is interchange. Interchange varies by the card type, MCC or merchant category and the product type." Target ~20% of spends, industry runs 20–25%: "We want to be at the lower end of the spectrum." Mix moved 21.92% → 20.33% QoQ; the ~10–11% print in Q1 FY26 was "because of the BPSP action, which had happened in February."

EMI / instalment lending ("spend to lend") — the strategic swing factor. "our focus primarily is on spend to lend… how the customer converts its spending into the EMI — either at the point of sale itself or after that." Infrastructure built over two years: "We have understanding and arrangements with almost all the OEM in the country", plus "all the payment gateways, PGs and intermediaries in between." In-app conversion: "at the first instance where there is the pay now button, along with it, it has pay in EMI… We see a good percentage of our spend, in double digits, which gets converted into instalments lending every month."

Revolver book — structurally softening. Revolver rate 22% in IBNEA, interest-earning assets ~55%. Management links the softness to PL competition: "that is one of the reasons why we have seen a slight reduction in the revolver rates as well."

UPI-on-credit / RuPay — the volume engine. "UPI on credit card usage has grown further by 13% quarter-over-quarter, especially in department stores, groceries, utilities, fuel, restaurant and apparel categories, driven by rupay and QR acceptance." Attributed to "a very focused strategy that we have employed towards the RuPay cards, where we have increased the number of RuPay cards. Those RuPay cards attachment on the different PSPs has been done."
Geography: "Tier 2 plus cities continue to contribute strongly to overall retail spend on the back of UPI on credit card spends."

Personal loan on card — evaluated, not launched. "some of our customers carry that asset. But to a new set of customers, at this point of time, we are refraining from offering that. We might look at it in the future"; "We are evaluating it… It's an internal evaluation."

Rental payments — deliberately suppressed, not a fee line. "the reason it got stopped was because there was no KYC being done of the end recipient, which in this case, is the landlord… acquiring banks have started doing KYC and are getting the landlords accepted, there the rentals have started, but that volume is very minimal. And we are not seeing any growth in that category… The idea is not to let this become large and keep them under control. So this was not an idea of making a fee income from these things. This is more of us stopping an incorrect activity."
growth verticals / optionality: EMI/instalment conversion as the yield defence against the personal-loan alternative — an explicitly priced-to-compete product: "the EMI product which is comparable in terms of pricing is something which we are working on as well." Mix effect on yield: "even when you are increasing your EMI component, the transactor portion is going down, that also adds to the yield overall."

Credit-limit rationalisation as a spend unlock. After two conservative years — "we have done a lot of rationalization of limits as well, maybe we were slightly conservative because we were going through a tough cycle." Clarified to mean increases: "By rationalization, I mean increasing the limit"; "limit sometime can be a constraint for boosting spend." Enabled by better income imputation: "we have been enhancing our analytics also off late, and we are in a better position to impute the income of the customer as well." Also a lever on interest income: "increasing credit lines… is one such strategy for people who are already holding an instalment lending book, so that they can purchase more."

Hyper-personalisation tech stack — "a large tech investment in the company last year… on hyper-personalization. So the ability to contact the customer individually, give offers" — credited with the 53% active rate (+1 pp) and retail-spend outperformance.
Premium + Banca-led acquisition: "grow Banca as a channel and acquire premium customers digitally with high spending patterns and good credit scores."
Tier 2 / Tier 3 expansion alongside metros; co-brand portfolio breadth "across all key sectors, including lifestyle, retail, travel."
Personal-loan-on-card as an unexercised product option (see §5).
FY28 ECL data-refresh tailwind (optionality, not guidance): "the way we are seeing improvement in the asset quality, the data refresh will lead to the release of ECL, which is already happening."
6a. moat & competitive position (optiona: Captive parent distribution (the "family silver"). "because we are a subsidiary of State Bank of India, and the bank has almost 53 crores plus customers… you still end up with at least 1.5 crores to 2 crores customers of the bank, which are cardable in that sense. The bank also has a large base of corporate salary package accounts, large base of home loan customers… So this is family silver that we work with." Quantified in the mix: ~47% of sourcing is Banca, against 53% open market — a distribution channel no non-bank issuer can replicate.

Scale position. "SBI Cards is the second largest credit card player in terms of cards in force, spends as well as transactions", with 18.6% share of cards in force and 19.5% share of spends — and spend share is rising (from 18.1% in FY26), i.e. share gain, not just scale.

OEM / payment-rail arrangements at the point of sale. "We have understanding and arrangements with almost all the OEM in the country, wherein we have offers for our customers at the point of sale or online. We also work with all the payment gateways, PGs and intermediaries in between, who are able to process the data and be able to give insights to us directly." A merchant-and-rail network that gates instalment conversion.

Co-brand franchise depth. "our core brand BPCL SBI Card crossed the 5 million milestone, making it one of the largest fuel co-branded credit card partnerships in India"; plus a newly-signed Flipkart co-brand.

Underwriting/analytics as a cycle-tested asset. "if you look at our entry rates, they are almost, I will say, decadal low. So the entry rates into the first bucket itself are very, very low" — evidenced, not asserted, by Stage 2 at 3.57% and Stage 2/3 "lowest post-COVID."
App engagement. "our mobile app, which is very highly rated. 4.5 and 4.6 on both iOS and Play Store" — the in-app "pay in EMI" placement is the conversion surface.
margins & cost dynamics: The margin bridge is squeezed from both ends. Portfolio yield 16%, cost of funds 6.6% (daily average, stable QoQ despite "volatility in interest rates in Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27"), NIM 10.8% — but NIM fell QoQ (analyst: "we have seen margins come off for quarter-on-quarter") and the prepared remarks guide cost of funds up: "we expect cost of funds to trend higher in line with the market rates." CEO on treasury: "In last quarter also as you know, treasury rates hiked up quite a bit. But I would say that the company could manage the cost of funds pretty well."

Cost-of-funds defence is sourcing-side, not pricing-side: "looking at what is the source of funding, which is the best pricing that we can get, what are the terms? And we will continue to scan the market accordingly and protect the NIMs going forward." Plus a partial pass-through: "any increase in cost of funds, also through benchmark change gets passed on to the incremental book that is being done" — incremental book only.
Yield defence is mix-driven: EMI share up + transactor share down = yield support; revolver rate (22%) has a "downward bias"; credit-line increases raise instalment-book capacity.

Opex is growing with volume and will worsen seasonally. "the operating expenses have been growing in line with the business growth, both in terms of new card sourcing that we are doing quarter-on-quarter higher and also the spend that the customers are making, there's a cost associated with that as well." An investor asked for an opex breakup in quarterly updates — "We'll evaluate that." Disclosure gap, worth re-asking.
Employee cost carries a one-off: new wage code past-service-cost provision (§2 note 5), unquantified.

Fee income mix: instance-based fees down on lower late fees; recovery expected "H2 onwards" on base effect, "not on account of late fee." Corporate cards are pure interchange, and interchange "varies by the card type, MCC or merchant category and the product type."
Cost-to-income: FY27 full-year 56–58%, Q3 seasonally higher on festive reward/marketing spend.
capex / expansion (watch slippage): Not a physical-capex business — no plant, commissioning date or capex number was given on the call. The equivalent "capex" lines disclosed:
Tech capex (already incurred): "a large tech investment in the company last year… on hyper-personalization" — no rupee figure.

Customer-acquisition spend is the real growth capex, and it is being stepped up: >1 million new accounts in Q1, "higher new acquisition from this quarter onwards", with the associated opex flagged as rising.
Reach expansion: "expand our reach in potential growth markets, including Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, along with the metros."
Capital position: capital adequacy 25.6%; "Our liquidity position continues to be strong." No capital raise discussed.
Slippage watch: the H2 FY27 receivables pick-up is the schedule to police — it has already been deferred once in framing (Q1 growth was ~2% QoQ against 27% YoY spend growth).
capital allocation: Thin on this call — no buyback, dividend, fund-raise, M&A or subsidiary restructuring was discussed. What is visible:
Capital adequacy 25.6%, described as "a healthy level"; no raise mentioned, no leverage target given.
Retained-earnings compounding is the implicit policy: ROE 16.5% (+72 bps YoY, +89 bps QoQ) with the stated medium-term ROA target of 4–4.5%.

Provision buffer policy: overlay drawn from INR220 cr → INR70 cr carried, held in Stage 1 for geopolitical risk — a conscious decision to release most, but not all, of the cushion into earnings this quarter.

Product-capital discipline: corporate cards deliberately capped at ~20% of spends because "in the absolute sense, the corporate card profitability is very low"; personal-loan-on-card withheld from new customers pending internal evaluation.
risks & watch-items: 1. Revenue growth is 3% while spends grew 27% — the monetisation gap. Receivables +3% YoY is the binding constraint on interest income; the whole FY27 thesis rests on an H2 pick-up that has not yet appeared.

2. Earnings quality — the ECL overlay drawdown. INR180 cr of a INR220 cr overlay consumed plus a INR65 cr release and a INR35 cr write-back inside a INR664 cr PAT quarter. Only INR70 cr of cushion remains; the same lever cannot be pulled twice at this size.
3. Cost of funds guided higher ("in line with the market rates") against a yield only defensible via mix. Pass-through is limited to the incremental book.

4. Personal-loan cannibalisation of the revolver — management conceded it: "if he has an option of lower-priced personal loan, he will take a personal loan… And that is why… the EMI product which is comparable in terms of pricing is something which we are working on."

5. Middle East conflict → fuel prices → customer cash flows. The explicit escape clause on credit-cost guidance: "We continue to remain watchful, particularly for any second order impact on fuel prices, inflation, and consequently, customer cash flows"; "subject to any adverse impact of Middle East conflict on the asset quality."
6. Unsecured-lending posture. "we are in the business of unsecured lending, and we will stay alert to any significant stress happening, and we'll take quick action if needed."

7. IT-sector job losses in South India — management refuted, but the analyst evidence is specific. Anand Dama (Nuvama): "on the ground, whatever check that we have done with multiple lenders and collection agencies, they tell us they are basically about 300 to 400 basis points, bucket delinquency has gone up in that pool." Pande: "We have not seen in our book"; "even for the IT sector, we did a separate analysis also. As of now, we are not seeing any concerns. But we monitor, we are monitoring." Verify next quarter.

8. Weak monsoon. "In this current year, monsoon is not so good" — management downplayed via low rural penetration: "In the rural areas, there are very few customers or minimal customers there. So the impact would — might not be seen immediately in the Q2, Q3."

9. Regulatory intensity in cards/payments. "The regulatory environment has also evolved significantly, with increased emphasis on responsible lending, customer suitability, digital resilience, cybersecurity and customer protection." Precedent for real P&L impact exists: the BPSP action of February cut corporate spend share to ~10–11% in Q1 FY26. No new hard-dated regulatory change (MDR/interchange or otherwise) was announced on this call.
10. Late fee is structurally capped — "Late fee will continue to remain at the level that it is" — removing a historic fee-growth lever.

11. Limit-increase / EMI-push runs against the two-year underwriting tightening. Management is loosening limits into a recovering book; the credit-cost improvement is only ~6 quarters old ("Delinquencies have reduced in this quarter too, as witnessed in the last 6 quarters").
12. Opex disclosure gap — no breakup of operating & other expenses despite it being "a large chunk of the expenses"; company will only "evaluate" providing one.
management quality / tone: Composed, data-led and unusually disciplined about refusing guidance — three separate declinations to quantify EMI growth, credit cost and receivables, while still giving directional commitments they can be held to (moderation in credit cost, H2 receivables growth, NIM held, cost-to-income 56–58%). Two credibility markers stand out. First, self-correction in real time: after an analyst pushed back on "rationalization" of limits, Pande said "let me correct myself. By rationalization, I mean increasing the limit" — a genuine clarification rather than a dodge. Second, direct engagement with hostile data: on the IT-jobs delinquency claim she neither dismissed nor spun it — "we also heard it. We also analysed our portfolio… we did a separate analysis also. As of now, we are not seeing any concerns. But we monitor." Answers were split cleanly by function (Budhiraja on spends/EMI/products, Mohanty on opex/cost-to-income/yield pass-through, Bishnoi on the provision stack), which reads as a management team that knows its own numbers. Mild negatives: the prepared remarks and the Q&A give different cost-of-funds signals (up vs "no much change") without anyone reconciling them; the opex-breakup request got a non-committal "We'll evaluate that"; and the prepared script's macro/awards preamble ran long relative to the business content. Tone on competition was notably non-defensive — on personal loans, "it's not that the personal loan product and credit card product cannot work together. There is tremendous opportunity for both."
non-obvious takeaways: 1. The 27% spend growth is not a 27% revenue event. Revenue grew 3%. Spend growth is running through UPI-on-credit and RuPay — low-interchange, transactor-heavy rails — while the interest-earning book grew ~2% QoQ. Spend market share (19.5%) is now a weaker proxy for SBICARD's earnings than it used to be.

2. The corporate-spend "recovery" is optically flattering. Corporate share went ~10–11% (Q1 FY26, post-BPSP) → 21.92% → 20.33%. But corporate is the least profitable book ("corporate card profitability is very low", interchange-only, no lending). A falling corporate share is arguably good for mix — the opposite of how a spend-share headline reads.

3. Consumer-durable price inflation is a hidden EMI tailwind. "in the last quarter, you would have seen that the prices of consumer durables have gone up. And the moment the large ticket size or consumer durable prices go up, the conversion rate to instalment lending also goes up along with it." An inflation input that helps this P&L.

4. The revolver decline is partly self-inflicted, by design. Management is deliberately migrating revolvers into cheaper EMI to defend against personal loans — trading headline revolver rate (22%, "downward bias") for retained wallet. The yield hit is intentional, not purely competitive loss.

5. "Rationalization" was a euphemism that ran the wrong way for two years. Limits were cut through the tough cycle; the same word now means increases. The spend-growth lever the market watches (limit headroom) has only just been switched back on.

6. Rental payments were killed by KYC, not by economics — and the volume migrated: "some of the cash out, moved to certain other categories like education and a couple of other categories where we started levying fees also." A quiet fee-line reshuffle inside "instance-based fees."

7. The FY28 ECL tailwind will come from data, not model. "Normally, we will not relax the model… Whatever changes will happen during the year will happen because of the data refresh." So the buffer release is mechanical and depends on delinquency flows continuing to improve — not a discretionary lever.

8. Personal loan is a product SBICARD chooses not to sell despite owning the cash-flow data. When an analyst pressed why, the answer was an unhedged "We are evaluating it… It's an internal evaluation." — i.e. an unexercised optionality with a known distribution and a known credit file.

9. Penetration math is the bull case management leads with, twice. 121 million cards but only "52 million to 55 million customers", against "350 million to 400 million" bureau-scoreable files and 1.5–2 crore "cardable" SBI customers. The industry constraint is stated to be acquisition, not credit availability.

10. Fuel-price risk cuts both ways here. BPCL SBI Card is the flagship co-brand (5 million cards, fuel spends) while fuel-price-driven cash-flow stress is management's named credit worry — the same variable is a spend driver and a delinquency driver.

guidance (critical — verify next quarter: Management repeatedly and explicitly refused numeric guidance this quarter: "we are not giving any guidance in terms of the numbers" (EMI); "As of now, I'm not giving any guidance in terms of the numbers" / "I'm refraining from giving any guidance in terms of the absolute numbers or percentage terms right now" (credit cost, receivables). What was given:

Receivables / asset growth: "We expect asset growth to pick up from the second half of financial year 2027, given higher new acquisition from this quarter onwards and festive season in Q3"; restated in Q&A — "in the second half of this year, we will see growth in receivables as well." (H2 FY27 = Oct-2026 → Mar-2027.)

Credit cost: "this trend of credit cost, will see some more moderation going forward"; on a peer's 3Q normalisation comment — "Normalization can be debated. But definitely, as I mentioned, we will moderate further in terms of credit cost." Caveated: "we expect the gross credit cost to stay within the current range, subject to any adverse impact of Middle East conflict on the asset quality."
ROA: "on track to achieve our stated ROA guidance of 4% to 4.5% in medium term" (medium-term, no date).
NIM: "I would say NIM should be around this range only… we should maintain the NIM around these levels."
Portfolio yield: "as we had guided that we will continue to keep the yield in a broad range."

Cost of funds: "we don't expect much change. It should remain somewhere in the similar range. Ultimately, it will depend to a very large extent on the policy action as well in terms of the T-bill rates" — but the prepared remarks said "we expect cost of funds to trend higher in line with the market rates." These two statements sit in tension; treat the prepared-remark version as the base case and flag it next quarter.

Cost-to-income: "We'll give you a yearly number, which is an average of all the 4 quarters. So it should be… in the range of about 56% to 58%" (FY27 full-year; reaffirming last quarter's indication). Q3 will be seasonally worse — "obviously, the festive season will definitely see a higher cost to income."

Corporate spend mix: "we would like it to be around 20% of our overall spend… It will be 20% plus minus"; can go below 20% — "We can take it below 20% also. We like to keep most of our spends profitable."
Revolver: "we expect the revolver to continue to be stable where they are right now… we have witnessed a little bit of a downward bias on the revolver. But they will stay in somewhat similar range."
Instance-based fees: "Once the base effect starts to come in, in H2 onwards, you will start seeing it go up but not on account of late fee. Late fee will continue to remain at the level that it is."
Opex: "we do expect that as the festive season comes in, these expenses will be higher."

ECL model: "Normally, we will not relax the model. At most, we may do some kind of an enhancement… Whatever changes will happen during the year will happen because of the data refresh" — i.e. any FY28 ECL tailwind comes from data refresh, not model loosening.
order book & pipeline: Not an order-book business. Forward pipeline proxies disclosed on the call:

New-account run-rate: >1 million new accounts in Q1 FY27 (+17% YoY); net card additions of 4.84 lakh, "highest in the industry for the quarter" per RBI data — the acquisition cohort that management says converts to receivables growth in H2 FY27.

Addressable market (two-legged, management's own framing): (a) Banca / "family silver" — SBI has "almost 53 crores plus customers", of which "you still end up with at least 1.5 crores to 2 crores customers of the bank, which are cardable", plus corporate salary-package and home-loan bases; (b) open market — co-brands, e.g. "Flipkart itself has close to more than 500 million customers on their transacting customers."

Bureau-scoreable universe: "there are at least 350 million to 400 million customers, where the files – and where the data is available, you can credit score those customers", against "India now has 121 million credit cards in circulation" and "We have hardly 52 million to 55 million customers in the country."
Co-brand milestone: "our core brand BPCL SBI Card crossed the 5 million milestone, making it one of the largest fuel co-branded credit card partnerships in India."
segment / subsidiary detail: Retail cards — the entire profit pool. "On an overall basis, in the absolute sense, the corporate card profitability is very low. Our profits are essentially on the retail card." Retail earns both fee and interest income.

Corporate / commercial cards — interchange-only, deliberately capped. "In corporate card spends, typically — we don't give lending options there. So the customer has to pay back the full outstanding balance. So primary source of income is interchange. Interchange varies by the card type, MCC or merchant category and the product type." Target ~20% of spends, industry runs 20–25%: "We want to be at the lower end of the spectrum." Mix moved 21.92% → 20.33% QoQ; the ~10–11% print in Q1 FY26 was "because of the BPSP action, which had happened in February."

EMI / instalment lending ("spend to lend") — the strategic swing factor. "our focus primarily is on spend to lend… how the customer converts its spending into the EMI — either at the point of sale itself or after that." Infrastructure built over two years: "We have understanding and arrangements with almost all the OEM in the country", plus "all the payment gateways, PGs and intermediaries in between." In-app conversion: "at the first instance where there is the pay now button, along with it, it has pay in EMI… We see a good percentage of our spend, in double digits, which gets converted into instalments lending every month."

Revolver book — structurally softening. Revolver rate 22% in IBNEA, interest-earning assets ~55%. Management links the softness to PL competition: "that is one of the reasons why we have seen a slight reduction in the revolver rates as well."

UPI-on-credit / RuPay — the volume engine. "UPI on credit card usage has grown further by 13% quarter-over-quarter, especially in department stores, groceries, utilities, fuel, restaurant and apparel categories, driven by rupay and QR acceptance." Attributed to "a very focused strategy that we have employed towards the RuPay cards, where we have increased the number of RuPay cards. Those RuPay cards attachment on the different PSPs has been done."
Geography: "Tier 2 plus cities continue to contribute strongly to overall retail spend on the back of UPI on credit card spends."

Personal loan on card — evaluated, not launched. "some of our customers carry that asset. But to a new set of customers, at this point of time, we are refraining from offering that. We might look at it in the future"; "We are evaluating it… It's an internal evaluation."

Rental payments — deliberately suppressed, not a fee line. "the reason it got stopped was because there was no KYC being done of the end recipient, which in this case, is the landlord… acquiring banks have started doing KYC and are getting the landlords accepted, there the rentals have started, but that volume is very minimal. And we are not seeing any growth in that category… The idea is not to let this become large and keep them under control. So this was not an idea of making a fee income from these things. This is more of us stopping an incorrect activity."
growth verticals / optionality: EMI/instalment conversion as the yield defence against the personal-loan alternative — an explicitly priced-to-compete product: "the EMI product which is comparable in terms of pricing is something which we are working on as well." Mix effect on yield: "even when you are increasing your EMI component, the transactor portion is going down, that also adds to the yield overall."

Credit-limit rationalisation as a spend unlock. After two conservative years — "we have done a lot of rationalization of limits as well, maybe we were slightly conservative because we were going through a tough cycle." Clarified to mean increases: "By rationalization, I mean increasing the limit"; "limit sometime can be a constraint for boosting spend." Enabled by better income imputation: "we have been enhancing our analytics also off late, and we are in a better position to impute the income of the customer as well." Also a lever on interest income: "increasing credit lines… is one such strategy for people who are already holding an instalment lending book, so that they can purchase more."

Hyper-personalisation tech stack — "a large tech investment in the company last year… on hyper-personalization. So the ability to contact the customer individually, give offers" — credited with the 53% active rate (+1 pp) and retail-spend outperformance.
Premium + Banca-led acquisition: "grow Banca as a channel and acquire premium customers digitally with high spending patterns and good credit scores."
Tier 2 / Tier 3 expansion alongside metros; co-brand portfolio breadth "across all key sectors, including lifestyle, retail, travel."
Personal-loan-on-card as an unexercised product option (see §5).
FY28 ECL data-refresh tailwind (optionality, not guidance): "the way we are seeing improvement in the asset quality, the data refresh will lead to the release of ECL, which is already happening."
6a. moat & competitive position (optiona: Captive parent distribution (the "family silver"). "because we are a subsidiary of State Bank of India, and the bank has almost 53 crores plus customers… you still end up with at least 1.5 crores to 2 crores customers of the bank, which are cardable in that sense. The bank also has a large base of corporate salary package accounts, large base of home loan customers… So this is family silver that we work with." Quantified in the mix: ~47% of sourcing is Banca, against 53% open market — a distribution channel no non-bank issuer can replicate.

Scale position. "SBI Cards is the second largest credit card player in terms of cards in force, spends as well as transactions", with 18.6% share of cards in force and 19.5% share of spends — and spend share is rising (from 18.1% in FY26), i.e. share gain, not just scale.

OEM / payment-rail arrangements at the point of sale. "We have understanding and arrangements with almost all the OEM in the country, wherein we have offers for our customers at the point of sale or online. We also work with all the payment gateways, PGs and intermediaries in between, who are able to process the data and be able to give insights to us directly." A merchant-and-rail network that gates instalment conversion.

Co-brand franchise depth. "our core brand BPCL SBI Card crossed the 5 million milestone, making it one of the largest fuel co-branded credit card partnerships in India"; plus a newly-signed Flipkart co-brand.

Underwriting/analytics as a cycle-tested asset. "if you look at our entry rates, they are almost, I will say, decadal low. So the entry rates into the first bucket itself are very, very low" — evidenced, not asserted, by Stage 2 at 3.57% and Stage 2/3 "lowest post-COVID."
App engagement. "our mobile app, which is very highly rated. 4.5 and 4.6 on both iOS and Play Store" — the in-app "pay in EMI" placement is the conversion surface.
margins & cost dynamics: The margin bridge is squeezed from both ends. Portfolio yield 16%, cost of funds 6.6% (daily average, stable QoQ despite "volatility in interest rates in Q4 FY26 and Q1 FY27"), NIM 10.8% — but NIM fell QoQ (analyst: "we have seen margins come off for quarter-on-quarter") and the prepared remarks guide cost of funds up: "we expect cost of funds to trend higher in line with the market rates." CEO on treasury: "In last quarter also as you know, treasury rates hiked up quite a bit. But I would say that the company could manage the cost of funds pretty well."

Cost-of-funds defence is sourcing-side, not pricing-side: "looking at what is the source of funding, which is the best pricing that we can get, what are the terms? And we will continue to scan the market accordingly and protect the NIMs going forward." Plus a partial pass-through: "any increase in cost of funds, also through benchmark change gets passed on to the incremental book that is being done" — incremental book only.
Yield defence is mix-driven: EMI share up + transactor share down = yield support; revolver rate (22%) has a "downward bias"; credit-line increases raise instalment-book capacity.

Opex is growing with volume and will worsen seasonally. "the operating expenses have been growing in line with the business growth, both in terms of new card sourcing that we are doing quarter-on-quarter higher and also the spend that the customers are making, there's a cost associated with that as well." An investor asked for an opex breakup in quarterly updates — "We'll evaluate that." Disclosure gap, worth re-asking.
Employee cost carries a one-off: new wage code past-service-cost provision (§2 note 5), unquantified.

Fee income mix: instance-based fees down on lower late fees; recovery expected "H2 onwards" on base effect, "not on account of late fee." Corporate cards are pure interchange, and interchange "varies by the card type, MCC or merchant category and the product type."
Cost-to-income: FY27 full-year 56–58%, Q3 seasonally higher on festive reward/marketing spend.
capex / expansion (watch slippage): Not a physical-capex business — no plant, commissioning date or capex number was given on the call. The equivalent "capex" lines disclosed:
Tech capex (already incurred): "a large tech investment in the company last year… on hyper-personalization" — no rupee figure.

Customer-acquisition spend is the real growth capex, and it is being stepped up: >1 million new accounts in Q1, "higher new acquisition from this quarter onwards", with the associated opex flagged as rising.
Reach expansion: "expand our reach in potential growth markets, including Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, along with the metros."
Capital position: capital adequacy 25.6%; "Our liquidity position continues to be strong." No capital raise discussed.
Slippage watch: the H2 FY27 receivables pick-up is the schedule to police — it has already been deferred once in framing (Q1 growth was ~2% QoQ against 27% YoY spend growth).
capital allocation: Thin on this call — no buyback, dividend, fund-raise, M&A or subsidiary restructuring was discussed. What is visible:
Capital adequacy 25.6%, described as "a healthy level"; no raise mentioned, no leverage target given.
Retained-earnings compounding is the implicit policy: ROE 16.5% (+72 bps YoY, +89 bps QoQ) with the stated medium-term ROA target of 4–4.5%.

Provision buffer policy: overlay drawn from INR220 cr → INR70 cr carried, held in Stage 1 for geopolitical risk — a conscious decision to release most, but not all, of the cushion into earnings this quarter.

Product-capital discipline: corporate cards deliberately capped at ~20% of spends because "in the absolute sense, the corporate card profitability is very low"; personal-loan-on-card withheld from new customers pending internal evaluation.
risks & watch-items: 1. Revenue growth is 3% while spends grew 27% — the monetisation gap. Receivables +3% YoY is the binding constraint on interest income; the whole FY27 thesis rests on an H2 pick-up that has not yet appeared.

2. Earnings quality — the ECL overlay drawdown. INR180 cr of a INR220 cr overlay consumed plus a INR65 cr release and a INR35 cr write-back inside a INR664 cr PAT quarter. Only INR70 cr of cushion remains; the same lever cannot be pulled twice at this size.
3. Cost of funds guided higher ("in line with the market rates") against a yield only defensible via mix. Pass-through is limited to the incremental book.

4. Personal-loan cannibalisation of the revolver — management conceded it: "if he has an option of lower-priced personal loan, he will take a personal loan… And that is why… the EMI product which is comparable in terms of pricing is something which we are working on."

5. Middle East conflict → fuel prices → customer cash flows. The explicit escape clause on credit-cost guidance: "We continue to remain watchful, particularly for any second order impact on fuel prices, inflation, and consequently, customer cash flows"; "subject to any adverse impact of Middle East conflict on the asset quality."
6. Unsecured-lending posture. "we are in the business of unsecured lending, and we will stay alert to any significant stress happening, and we'll take quick action if needed."

7. IT-sector job losses in South India — management refuted, but the analyst evidence is specific. Anand Dama (Nuvama): "on the ground, whatever check that we have done with multiple lenders and collection agencies, they tell us they are basically about 300 to 400 basis points, bucket delinquency has gone up in that pool." Pande: "We have not seen in our book"; "even for the IT sector, we did a separate analysis also. As of now, we are not seeing any concerns. But we monitor, we are monitoring." Verify next quarter.

8. Weak monsoon. "In this current year, monsoon is not so good" — management downplayed via low rural penetration: "In the rural areas, there are very few customers or minimal customers there. So the impact would — might not be seen immediately in the Q2, Q3."

9. Regulatory intensity in cards/payments. "The regulatory environment has also evolved significantly, with increased emphasis on responsible lending, customer suitability, digital resilience, cybersecurity and customer protection." Precedent for real P&L impact exists: the BPSP action of February cut corporate spend share to ~10–11% in Q1 FY26. No new hard-dated regulatory change (MDR/interchange or otherwise) was announced on this call.
10. Late fee is structurally capped — "Late fee will continue to remain at the level that it is" — removing a historic fee-growth lever.

11. Limit-increase / EMI-push runs against the two-year underwriting tightening. Management is loosening limits into a recovering book; the credit-cost improvement is only ~6 quarters old ("Delinquencies have reduced in this quarter too, as witnessed in the last 6 quarters").
12. Opex disclosure gap — no breakup of operating & other expenses despite it being "a large chunk of the expenses"; company will only "evaluate" providing one.
management quality / tone: Composed, data-led and unusually disciplined about refusing guidance — three separate declinations to quantify EMI growth, credit cost and receivables, while still giving directional commitments they can be held to (moderation in credit cost, H2 receivables growth, NIM held, cost-to-income 56–58%). Two credibility markers stand out. First, self-correction in real time: after an analyst pushed back on "rationalization" of limits, Pande said "let me correct myself. By rationalization, I mean increasing the limit" — a genuine clarification rather than a dodge. Second, direct engagement with hostile data: on the IT-jobs delinquency claim she neither dismissed nor spun it — "we also heard it. We also analysed our portfolio… we did a separate analysis also. As of now, we are not seeing any concerns. But we monitor." Answers were split cleanly by function (Budhiraja on spends/EMI/products, Mohanty on opex/cost-to-income/yield pass-through, Bishnoi on the provision stack), which reads as a management team that knows its own numbers. Mild negatives: the prepared remarks and the Q&A give different cost-of-funds signals (up vs "no much change") without anyone reconciling them; the opex-breakup request got a non-committal "We'll evaluate that"; and the prepared script's macro/awards preamble ran long relative to the business content. Tone on competition was notably non-defensive — on personal loans, "it's not that the personal loan product and credit card product cannot work together. There is tremendous opportunity for both."
non-obvious takeaways: 1. The 27% spend growth is not a 27% revenue event. Revenue grew 3%. Spend growth is running through UPI-on-credit and RuPay — low-interchange, transactor-heavy rails — while the interest-earning book grew ~2% QoQ. Spend market share (19.5%) is now a weaker proxy for SBICARD's earnings than it used to be.

2. The corporate-spend "recovery" is optically flattering. Corporate share went ~10–11% (Q1 FY26, post-BPSP) → 21.92% → 20.33%. But corporate is the least profitable book ("corporate card profitability is very low", interchange-only, no lending). A falling corporate share is arguably good for mix — the opposite of how a spend-share headline reads.

3. Consumer-durable price inflation is a hidden EMI tailwind. "in the last quarter, you would have seen that the prices of consumer durables have gone up. And the moment the large ticket size or consumer durable prices go up, the conversion rate to instalment lending also goes up along with it." An inflation input that helps this P&L.

4. The revolver decline is partly self-inflicted, by design. Management is deliberately migrating revolvers into cheaper EMI to defend against personal loans — trading headline revolver rate (22%, "downward bias") for retained wallet. The yield hit is intentional, not purely competitive loss.

5. "Rationalization" was a euphemism that ran the wrong way for two years. Limits were cut through the tough cycle; the same word now means increases. The spend-growth lever the market watches (limit headroom) has only just been switched back on.

6. Rental payments were killed by KYC, not by economics — and the volume migrated: "some of the cash out, moved to certain other categories like education and a couple of other categories where we started levying fees also." A quiet fee-line reshuffle inside "instance-based fees."

7. The FY28 ECL tailwind will come from data, not model. "Normally, we will not relax the model… Whatever changes will happen during the year will happen because of the data refresh." So the buffer release is mechanical and depends on delinquency flows continuing to improve — not a discretionary lever.

8. Personal loan is a product SBICARD chooses not to sell despite owning the cash-flow data. When an analyst pressed why, the answer was an unhedged "We are evaluating it… It's an internal evaluation." — i.e. an unexercised optionality with a known distribution and a known credit file.

9. Penetration math is the bull case management leads with, twice. 121 million cards but only "52 million to 55 million customers", against "350 million to 400 million" bureau-scoreable files and 1.5–2 crore "cardable" SBI customers. The industry constraint is stated to be acquisition, not credit availability.

10. Fuel-price risk cuts both ways here. BPCL SBI Card is the flagship co-brand (5 million cards, fuel spends) while fuel-price-driven cash-flow stress is management's named credit worry — the same variable is a spend driver and a delinquency driver.
